title: Book: Thinking, Fast and Slow — Daniel Kahneman (2011)
publisher: Artha Kavach original summary of a book's ideas (paraphrase, not a quotation; the author's opinion, not settled fact) — pending manual verification
text: Nobel laureate Daniel Kahneman describes two modes of thinking: System 1, fast, intuitive and emotional, and System 2, slow, deliberate and effortful. Many money mistakes come from System 1. Key biases: loss aversion (a loss hurts more than an equal gain pleases, which makes people sell in panic or hold losers), anchoring (being swayed by an arbitrary first number such as a past price or a 'discount'), overconfidence, the sunk-cost fallacy, and the availability bias (overweighting vivid news). Practical defences: automate decisions, slow down before big ones, use checklists, avoid checking your portfolio daily and compare with base rates. Caveats: some of the book's psychology findings, especially on priming, have not replicated well, but its core on loss aversion and judgement biases remains influential.
